scenes.name: US Festival 1983 y el renacimiento del heavy
scenes.book: Heavy Metal: The Music and Its Culture
scenes.author: Deena Weinstein
scenes.desc: A principios de los ochenta la prensa rock habla de «revival» o «renacimiento» del heavy (Creem, octubre de 1980: el género «había hecho un Jesucristo»): nacen bandas en todo el mundo, las veteranas tocan para públicos mucho mayores y los medios se abren al metal. La señal más pública es el US Festival de 1983, patrocinado por Steve Wozniak: el día dedicado al heavy, con Ozzy, Judas Priest, Mötley Crüe, Scorpions, Quiet Riot, Van Halen y Triumph, reunió mucho más público que los otros dos.

podcast.body: Triumph was formed in 1975 by Rick Emmett, Gil Moore, and Mike Levine. "It was Rick Emmett, Gil Moore and Mike Levine who formed triumphant in 1975."

podcast.title: First US Performance (1978)
podcast.body: Triumph's inaugural performance in America took place in San Antonio in 1978, drawing an audience of approximately 6,000 people, which constituted their largest crowd up to that point. "Their first performance in America was in front of about 6,000 people in San Antonio in 1978, which was their largest crowd to date."

podcast.title: "It's All Done with Mirrors" Philosophy
podcast.body: Mike Levine articulated a philosophy that perception was crucial in the music industry, stating, "It's all done with mirrors." He elaborated that people were often more impressed by what they heard (or perceived) than by what they actually saw. "Levine said it was a big deal when we came back to Canada record companies in the US started paying attention to us. It's all done with mirrors. People are far more impressed with what they hear than with what they see."

podcast.title: Beneficiary of FM Radio Rules
podcast.body: Triumph was a band that benefited from Canada's changed FM radio rules in the 1960s, which required stations to play more album-oriented rock and a 30% Canadian content quota. This provided more airplay opportunities for established Canadian bands. "This helped out bands like Rush Triumph in April wine."

podcast.title: Cancon Boosted Success (1970s)
podcast.body: Triumph was among the many homegrown rock talents whose careers were boosted by the Cancon rules in the 1970s, contributing to Canadian success stories and, in some instances, international success. "Just on the rock side, we had Rush, April Wine, the Guess Who, Triumph, Crobar, Teenage Head, Max Webster, Chilowac, FM, Saga, and a foot-and-cold water."

podcast.title: Commercial Success Despite Critical Failure
podcast.body: Triumph achieved significant commercial success, selling millions of records, cassettes, CDs, and concert tickets, largely to a demographic of "mostly straight white male dudes who gravitated to arena rock." This success came despite a general lack of critical acclaim. "the mostly straight white male dudes who gravitated to arena rock bought their records and cassettes and CDs and concert tickets by the millions and made triumphant others like them a success even if they were not critically successful."

podcast.title: Critical Reception
podcast.body: Initially, critics struggled to identify unique qualities in Triumph, often finding little to distinguish them from other rock or hard rock bands. "critics really couldn't find much that distinguished triumphant from any other rock band or hard rock band out there."

podcast.title: Derivative Sound Accusation
podcast.body: Triumph's sound was frequently criticized and dismissed as derivative, to which the band countered by asserting that "everything is derivative at least in rock," suggesting that originality within the genre was inherently limited. "Triumphs sound was dismissed as derivative to which the band said yes, it is everything is derivative at least in rock"

podcast.title: Early Success and Domestic Acceptance
podcast.body: Triumph had success as far back as the 1960s, but like many Canadian groups, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after they had a hit in America. This pattern highlights the historical bias where external validation was crucial for Canadian artists at home. "The guests who BTO Rush, Triumph, April Wine and others had success as far back as the 1960s. But in most cases, domestic acceptance and popularity only came after these groups had a hit in America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Emphasis on Accessibility
podcast.body: According to Rick Emmett, Triumph consistently aimed for accessibility in their music, a contrast to Rush, intending to offer "loud arena rock that you could sink your teeth into" for audiences who preferred music that didn't require deep intellectual engagement. "Emmett said that triumphant was always trying to be accessible in a way that rush was not."

podcast.title: Loyal Fanbase and Arena Shows
podcast.body: Despite critical dismissal, Triumph cultivated a devoted fanbase. Interviews from decades later still highlight the loyalty of their fans and how the enthusiastic reactions at their arena shows served as a significant motivation for the band. "They had a following though and even now if you listen to Emma and more interviews looking back 45, 50 years ago they will talk about the loyalty of the fans and how the reaction of the fans that their arena shows motivated them."

podcast.title: Quintessential Arena Rock Performances
podcast.body: Triumph's concerts were archetypal arena rock shows, characterized by elaborate use of "fireworks and lights," and consistently grew in scale and spectacle. "Their shows were the quintessential arena shows with fireworks and lights and all that and they always seem to get bigger and bigger."

podcast.title: US Record Label Attention Post-Canadian Return
podcast.body: Mike Levine of Triumph noted that after the band returned to Canada following their first significant US performance, American record companies began to pay attention to them, suggesting a perception that US exposure was necessary to gain industry interest back home. "Levine said it was a big deal when we came back to Canada record companies in the US started paying attention to us."

xref.title: First Professional Internet-Only Concert (1994)
xref.body: On November 10, 1994, this Seattle group made history by performing what is believed to be the first-ever Internet-only concert by a professional band. Despite the technical challenges, which resulted in a "messy and glitchy" broadcast with poor audio, the event was lauded as a significant "technological triumph" and a pioneering step for webcasts and streaming. "The answer seems to be a Seattle group called SkyCriseMary on November 10th, 1994. It was messy and glitchy and the audio was bad, but it made history. It was a technological triumph."

xref.title: Eddie Vedder Was a Child Model – Department Store Catalogs, TV Commercials, Bozo the Clown
xref.body: Growing up in Chicago, Eddie's mother entered him in photo shoots and TV commercial auditions. He appeared in at least five department store catalogs (including Bloomingdale's) modeling back-to-school clothing as a five-year-old, and appeared in TV commercials for Hallmark greeting cards and Chuckles candy. He was one of the kids driving a Big Wheel in a commercial that ran during Saturday morning cartoons. His biggest triumph was an appearance on the nationally broadcast *Bozo the Clown* show in the early 1970s. "He would rather not be known as the cute child model for Bloomingdale's."

xref.title: Financial Success of "In Rainbows" Model
xref.body: The unconventional "tip jar" approach for "In Rainbows" was a financial triumph for Radiohead. They estimated that the net revenue from this direct-to-fan digital release exceeded what they had earned from their seven previous albums combined, which were released through EMI. "Radio head estimates that the net they received for In Rainbows was bigger than for the seven albums they recorded for EMI."

xref.title: Founding and Expansion
xref.body: Metalworks first came online in 1978, established by the band Triumph in a non-descript industrial plaza in Mississauga, West of Toronto. Triumph built the studio to avoid the time pressures of recording in external facilities, and the complex expanded significantly over the years. "It first went online in 1978, when the band Triumph didn't want the time pressures of recording in someone else's studio, and over the years, the complex got bigger and bigger and bigger."

xref.title: Missed American Tour and Triumph
xref.body: Ian Curtis committed suicide just hours before Joy Division was scheduled to embark on their very first American tour. This tragic event occurred on the eve of what was perceived as a potential "gigantic, artistic, and commercial triumph" for the group. "Ian Curtis hung himself literally just hours before Joy Division was supposed to leave on their very first American tour."
